title: Given an array of distinct integers, return all possible subsets (the power set) using backtracking.
shortTitle: Subsets: include or exclude each element
keyPoints: The power set contains all 2^n subsets of an n-element array, including the empty set.
Use backtracking with a start index: record the current path at every node, not just at leaves.
Advancing the start index by one prevents reusing earlier elements and avoids generating permutations.
Time is O(n * 2^n) because there are 2^n subsets and copying each costs up to n.
An equivalent iterative approach uses bitmask enumeration over 0 to 2^n - 1.
This is the foundational backtracking pattern from which subsets-with-duplicates and combinations extend.

s1_definition.oneliner: For each element choose include or exclude; record the path at every step to get all 2^n subsets.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Power set** – the set of all subsets, including the empty set and the full set.
- **Backtracking** – a recursive helper carries a start index and the current partial subset.
- **Record at every node** – add a copy of the current path at every recursion level, not only at leaves.
- **Start index** – advancing by one prevents reusing earlier elements, generating subsets instead of permutations.
- **O(n * 2^n)** – 2^n subsets, each copied in up to O(n) time.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India offers n optional add-on services for a savings account. A customer can pick any combination: none, some, or all. Listing every possible package is listing the power set. For each add-on, Priya branches into "include it" and "leave it out," and every combination is a valid package.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Backtracking tree for [Locker, Insurance, Overdraft]:

  [] ← record
  ├── [Locker] ← record
  │   ├── [Locker, Insurance] ← record
  │   │   └── [Locker, Insurance, Overdraft] ← record
  │   └── [Locker, Overdraft] ← record
  ├── [Insurance] ← record
  │   └── [Insurance, Overdraft] ← record
  └── [Overdraft] ← record

  Total: 2^3 = 8 subsets
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Subsets, or the power set, is the foundational backtracking problem. I use a recursive helper that carries a start index and the current partial subset, and I record a copy of the path at every node of the recursion, not only at the leaves. Inside the loop I take an element, recurse with the next index, and then remove it to backtrack.

Advancing the start index by one prevents reusing earlier elements and stops me from generating permutations of the same subset. The whole thing is O(n times 2^n).

In my project at National Bank of India, the product team needed to enumerate every possible package of optional account add-ons to price each combination. When an interviewer prefers an iterative approach, I mention bitmask enumeration over 0 to 2^n - 1.

Remember one sentence: record the path at every node, use start+1 to prevent reuse, and you get all 2^n subsets.
